title: Diffusion current and the field that cancels it
prompt:
$D_n = 36$ cm²/s. In a silicon layer the electron density drops linearly from $2.7 \times 10^{16}$ cm⁻³ to $10^{15}$ cm⁻³ over 2 µm.

(6.14) What electron diffusion current density does this gradient cause? (6.15) What field over the 2 µm would make the electron drift flux cancel the diffusion flux ($\mu_n = 1350$ cm²/Vs)?

steps.title: Gradient in consistent units
steps.body: $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}n}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{10^{15} - 2.7 \times 10^{16}}{2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{cm}} = -1.3 \times 10^{20}\ \mathrm{cm^{-4}}$
steps.why: Densities are in cm⁻³ and D in cm²/s, so the distance must be in cm. 2 µm = 2 × 10⁻⁴ cm.

steps.title: Diffusion current
steps.body: $J_{n,\mathrm{diff}} = qD_n\frac{\mathrm{d}n}{\mathrm{d}x}$, magnitude $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 36 \times 1.3 \times 10^{20} = 749$ A/cm².
steps.why: Units: C × cm²/s × cm⁻⁴ = C s⁻¹ cm⁻² = A/cm². The sign is negative: electrons diffuse in +x, so the current points in −x.

steps.title: Drift that balances it
steps.body: Set $qn\mu_n\xi = J_{n,\mathrm{diff}}$: $\xi = \dfrac{749}{1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{15} \times 1350} = 3468$ V/cm.
steps.why: The answer book uses $n = 10^{15}$ cm⁻³. Because n varies across the layer, the balancing field is not uniform: at $2.7 \times 10^{16}$ cm⁻³ it would be 128 V/cm.

answer: (6.14) $|J_{n,\mathrm{diff}}| = 749$ A/cm² (750 with q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). (6.15) $\xi = 3468$ V/cm, directed from low to high density.
note: See the flag on page: ex. 6.15 is ambiguous about which density to use; the official answer takes the lowest value.

title: From irradiance to excess carriers in a wafer
prompt: A 100 µm p-type c-Si wafer is illuminated with 650 nm light, 1000 W/m². $\tilde n = 3.84 - 0.015i$, $\alpha = 4\pi k/\lambda$, $D_n = 29$ cm²/s, $L_n = 60$ µm. Steady state, low injection, uniform illumination, no current. Find (a) α, (b) R, (c) Φ at x = 0 and 50 µm, (d) $G_L$ at 50 µm, (e) Δn at 50 µm.

steps.title: (a) Absorption coefficient
steps.body: $\alpha = \dfrac{4\pi \times 0.015}{650 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}} = 2.9 \times 10^5$ m⁻¹.
steps.why: Only the imaginary part k determines absorption; the sign convention (n − ik here, n + iκ on the sheet) does not matter.

steps.title: (b) Reflectance
steps.why: Week 1: normal-incidence Fresnel reflectance. The tiny k hardly changes R.

steps.title: (c) Photon flux
steps.why: Lambert–Beer for photons. $\alpha x = 2.9 \times 10^5 \times 5 \times 10^{-5} = 14.5$: only one photon in two million survives to 50 µm.

steps.title: (d) Generation rate
steps.body: $G_L(50\ \mathrm{µm}) = \alpha\,\Phi(50\ \mathrm{µm}) = 2.9 \times 10^5 \times 1.08 \times 10^{15} = 3.1 \times 10^{20}$ m⁻³s⁻¹.
steps.why: Each absorbed photon makes one pair. The number absorbed per unit depth is $-\mathrm{d}\Phi/\mathrm{d}x = \alpha\Phi$.

steps.title: (e) Excess minority carriers
steps.body: With no current and steady state, the continuity equation reduces to $0 = G_L - \Delta n/\tau_n$. Lifetime: $\tau_n = L_n^2/D_n = (60 \times 10^{-4})^2/29 = 1.24$ µs. So $\Delta n = G_L\tau_n = 3.9 \times 10^{14}$ m⁻³ $= 3.9 \times 10^8$ cm⁻³.
steps.why: Low injection: the recombination rate of the minority electrons is $\Delta n/\tau_n$. No diffusion and no drift terms, because no current flows.

note: The answer book gives Φ(50 µm) = 1.14 × 10¹⁵ m⁻²s⁻¹, G = 3.3 × 10²⁰ m⁻³s⁻¹ and Δn = 4.1 × 10¹⁴ m⁻³: it uses $e^{-14.5} = 5.3 \times 10^{-7}$ instead of 5.0 × 10⁻⁷. It also remarks that $L_n$ and $D_n$ ‘should have been given’; instruction 2 does give them.

title: Doped silicon at room temperature and at 727 °C
prompt: A 10 × 10 × 10 cm³ c-Si slab contains $1.5 \times 10^{19}$ P atoms. $N_C \approx 6.2 \times 10^{15}T^{3/2}$, $N_V \approx 3.5 \times 10^{15}T^{3/2}$ cm⁻³, $E_G = 1.1$ eV, $5 \times 10^{22}$ atoms/cm³. (a) P density and ppm; (b) n, p, nᵢ; (c) $E_C - E_F$; (d) type; (e) the same at 727 °C; (f) why the difference; (g) band diagrams; (h) doping for $J_{drift} = 110$ A/cm² in p-type Si with $\mu_p = 470$ cm²/Vs, ξ = 25 V/cm.

steps.title: (a) Density
steps.body: $N_D = 1.5 \times 10^{19}/1000\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 1.5 \times 10^{16}$ cm⁻³; per million Si atoms: $1.5 \times 10^{16}/5 \times 10^{22} \times 10^6 = 0.3$ ppm.
steps.why: Doping is a tiny fraction: 3 phosphorus atoms per 10 million silicon atoms.

steps.title: (b) Carriers at 300 K
steps.why: $E_G = 1.1$ eV (not 1.12) is why $n_i$ is a bit higher than the usual 10¹⁰.

steps.title: (c), (d) Fermi level and type
steps.body: $E_C - E_F = k_BT\ln(N_C/n) = 0.02585\ln(3.22 \times 10^{19}/1.5 \times 10^{16}) = 0.20$ eV. n-type; electrons are the majority carriers.
steps.why: Intrinsic level: 0.557 eV below $E_C$. $E_F$ lies 0.36 eV above it.

steps.title: (e) At 727 °C = 1000 K
steps.why: Now n ≈ p: the slab is effectively intrinsic (very slightly n-type). Don't use n ≈ N_D when nᵢ is not small compared with N_D.

steps.title: (f), (g) Interpretation
steps.body: At 1000 K thermal energy breaks so many Si–Si bonds that the thermally generated electron–hole pairs (2.5 × 10¹⁷ cm⁻³) outnumber the donor electrons (1.5 × 10¹⁶). Band diagrams: at 300 K $E_F$ (dashed) close to $E_C$ (0.20 eV below); at 1000 K $E_F$ at the intrinsic level, 0.57 eV below $E_C$, near midgap.
steps.why: This is why semiconductor devices stop working when they get too hot.

steps.title: (h) Doping for a drift current
steps.body: $J = qp\mu_p\xi$ → $N_A \approx p = \dfrac{110}{1.602 \times 10^{-19} \times 470 \times 25} = 5.8 \times 10^{16}$ cm⁻³.
steps.why: In p-type material only the holes contribute noticeably.

note: Self-derived, not official: instruction 3 has no official answers yet. Computed and cross-checked with scripts (the profiles also with a numerical solver); compare with the official answers when they are published.

title: Illuminated strip, infinite lifetime
prompt: n-type semiconductor; constant excess generation $G_0$ for $-L < x < L$, none outside. Infinite minority-carrier lifetime, $\Delta p = 0$ at $x = \pm 3L$, low injection, no field. Find the steady-state $\Delta p(x)$.

steps.title: Equation per region
steps.body: Steady state, no field, τ → ∞: $D_p\Delta p'' + G(x) = 0$. Inside: $\Delta p'' = -G_0/D_p$. Outside: $\Delta p'' = 0$.
steps.why: With infinite lifetime the recombination term $\Delta p/\tau$ vanishes; only diffusion and generation remain.

steps.title: General solutions
steps.body: Inside: $\Delta p = -\frac{G_0}{2D_p}x^2 + C$ (symmetric, so no linear term). Outside ($x > 0$): $\Delta p = A(3L - x)$, already zero at $3L$.
steps.why: The problem is symmetric about $x = 0$, so the slope at the centre is zero.

steps.title: Match at x = L
steps.body: Slope: $-G_0L/D_p = -A$ → $A = G_0L/D_p$. Value: $-\frac{G_0L^2}{2D_p} + C = 2AL$ → $C = \frac{5G_0L^2}{2D_p}$.
steps.why: The density and the diffusion flux (∝ slope) must be continuous: no carriers appear or vanish at the boundary.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: $\Delta p(x) = \frac{G_0}{2D_p}(5L^2 - x^2)$ for $|x| \leq L$, and $\frac{G_0L}{D_p}(3L - |x|)$ for $L \leq |x| \leq 3L$. Maximum $2.5\,G_0L^2/D_p$ at $x = 0$.
steps.why: Check: total generation $2G_0L$ per unit area must leave through both ends: flux $D_p \times G_0L/D_p = G_0L$ at each end. ✓

answer: $\Delta p(x) = \dfrac{G_0}{2D_p}(5L^2 - x^2)$ for $|x| \leq L$; $\Delta p(x) = \dfrac{G_0L}{D_p}(3L - |x|)$ for $L \leq |x| \leq 3L$.
note: Self-derived, not official: instruction 3 has no official answers yet. Computed and cross-checked with scripts (the profiles also with a numerical solver); compare with the official answers when they are published.

title: Uniform generation in a bar with surface recombination
prompt: p-type c-Si bar of width W, uniform generation $G_L$, minority diffusion constant $D_n$, equilibrium density $n_0$. Steady state, no field, $n(0) = 0$, surface recombination velocity S at $x = W$. (a) Δn(x) for τ = ∞ and S = 0; (b) for τ = ∞ and S > 0; (c) sketch both.

steps.title: Equation and general solution
steps.body: $D_n\Delta n'' = -G_L$ → $\Delta n(x) = -\frac{G_L}{2D_n}x^2 + C_1x + C_0$. At $x = 0$: $n = 0$, so $\Delta n(0) = -n_0$ and $C_0 = -n_0$.
steps.why: $n_0$ is tiny in p-type silicon, so $\Delta n(0) \approx 0$; many textbook versions simply use $\Delta n(0) = 0$.

steps.title: (a) S = 0
steps.body: No surface recombination means no flow into the surface: $\Delta n'(W) = 0$ → $C_1 = G_LW/D_n$: $\Delta n(x) = \frac{G_L}{D_n}\left(Wx - \frac{x^2}{2}\right) - n_0$.
steps.why: A parabola with its top at the wall: all generated carriers diffuse back to $x = 0$.

steps.title: (b) S > 0
steps.body: Flux into the surface equals surface recombination: $-D_n\Delta n'(W) = S\,\Delta n(W)$. Substituting: $C_1 = \dfrac{G_LW(1 + \frac{SW}{2D_n}) + Sn_0}{D_n + SW}$.
steps.why: Checks: $S \to 0$ gives (a); $S \to \infty$ gives $\Delta n(W) = 0$, as at a contact.

steps.title: (c) Sketch
steps.body: Both start at ≈ 0. (a) rises to its maximum $G_LW^2/2D_n$ at $x = W$ with zero slope. (b) lies below (a) everywhere, peaks inside the bar at $x^* = C_1D_n/G_L$ and drops towards $x = W$.
steps.why: The larger $SW/D_n$, the more the right end is pulled down; the diagram on this page shows it live.

answer: (a) $\Delta n = \frac{G_L}{D_n}(Wx - \frac{x^2}{2}) - n_0$. (b) $\Delta n = -\frac{G_L}{2D_n}x^2 + C_1x - n_0$ with $C_1 = \frac{G_LW(1 + SW/2D_n) + Sn_0}{D_n + SW}$.
note: Self-derived, not official: instruction 3 has no official answers yet. Computed and cross-checked with scripts (the profiles also with a numerical solver); compare with the official answers when they are published. The boundary condition at x = 0 is read as n(0) = 0 (Δn(0) = −n₀), see the flag on this page.
